rv.q: For all its clear-eyed examination of certain kinds of meanness—the most insidious of which look a lot like caring—Straight White Men isn’t a mean play, and that feels like one of the most important things about it right now.
Young Jean Lee's 'Straight White Men' is a wrenching, funny and ultimately devastating examination of what happens when good intentions collide with systemic inequity.
'Straight White Men,' a smart, funny and affecting play that reaffirms Lee's status as one of the most important playwrights working today.
Lee is happy to let it burn...Lee is clever enough to know that.
Lee deftly captures the family's rhythms as they oscillate from teasing to concern to argument, breaking the tension with humour and physicality
This contextualization gives a touch of edge to a play that is otherwise quite square.

In fact, the 90-minute examination of the ingrained dynamics at work amongst an aging father and his three adult sons is, in large part, exactly those things Lee points to as so currently unfashionable: It’s nuanced, curious, and compassionate.

In deconstructing the lives of these white men with all their privilege and power, Lee discovers hidden levels of deep discontent — let's bite the bullet and call it unhappiness — that indicates the kind of existential human pain common to the human condition.
The play's indictment of privilege is nuanced and thoughtful, even if the dramatic payoff is somewhat unsatisfying.
That said, “Straight White Men” is still an exceedingly odd — and thus welcome — presence on Broadway.

It is also a missed opportunity play.
I can't really express how full and rich Straight White Men turned out to be for me.
This brisk, entertaining, and deeply thought-provoking play is never strident or sentimental.
The play becomes riveting despite its contrivances and unanswered questions.
Under Anna D. Shapiro’s assured direction, Armie Hammer, Josh Charles, and Paul Schneider have all fully inhabited their characters; and they emerge as a family, warts and all.
We, as the audience, join in with these fantastical creatures, debating and discussing what this unique and exciting new play is trying to tell us.

“The direction and acting are polished and confident...Shapiro and her vibrant cast infuse zest and sting into what could have been a staged doctoral thesis...Not much happens for the first hour or so in the way of plot...The play is a weird blend of traditional family drama in the Arthur Miller vein, and a meta-view of those plays.
Half a really funny play doesn't quite make up for the other half which is exaggerated baloney.
Lee has never been one for easy answers, but here she seems to resist even posing more pointed questions.
Straight White Men comes off as remarkably conventional, despite what seem like doth-protest-too-much attempts to market it as dark, edgy, and more challenging than it actually is.
Under Shapiro's steady hand, all three actors appear totally comfortable onstage and deliver performances that go far beyond cameo status.
Straight White Men is a powerful piece of theater that asks the same universal questions Matt is asking about his own identity.
What we are left here with not so much as a rewarding play but an unfulfilling setup of a premise.

cn.t: Mixed reviews greet Lee's historic Broadway debut, with critics praising the strong cast and thought-provoking examination of privilege, but finding the play's satirical punch underwhelming and its intentions unclear.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on Rows B to H center as the best views in Broadway's smallest house (597 seats), where the intimate scale means these seats feel closer to the stage than premium orchestra in any other Broadway theater. The Hayes-specific tradeoff: patrons repeatedly flag that the stage sits unusually high for such an intimate room, so Row A and the very front can force neck-craning — one AVFMS viewer described the Hayes stage as 'particularly high for the first couple of rows, so you'll be using your neck to look up,' and a JOB patron noted 'The stage is high so you don't see actors' feet.' Rows B-H sit far enough back to clear that stage-height issue while still letting you read facial expressions in a house this small.

sg.vl: Value sweet spot where the rake kicks in
sg.ra: Rows F-M center are consistently flagged as the value band at Hayes — priced below premium but still close in a 597-seat room. The Hayes-specific reason to favor the back half of that band (J-M) over F-I: an AVFMS reviewer explicitly observed that 'Row J in the orchestra level is where the rake of the floor starts to increase so even a short guy like me can see over someone tall.' That makes J-M the first rows where a tall head in front stops being a problem, which matters more at Hayes than at larger houses because the orchestra is 'more long than it is wide' (NYTix) and the stage height is tall, so front-orchestra sightlines are flatter than usual.

The very back row of the Hayes mezzanine sits directly against the theater's staff/operations area — a quirk specific to this post-2018-renovation layout. Multiple AVFMS reviewers independently complain the ushers or crew are audible throughout the show from Mezz Row J: one wrote 'this row butts up against the row where the theater staff sits and they chatted, loudly, throughout the show'; another said 'the ushers downstairs were loud and I could sometimes hear their murmurings'; an accessible-seat user at Mezz J-101 reported 'there's some sort of operation booth to the right of this seat and it's very loud and distracting. I could hear talking and typing throughout the entire show.' Because Hayes is the smallest house on Broadway, there's no orchestra noise to mask ambient staff chatter the way a 1,500-seat venue would — in this intimate room, the booth chatter carries.
